concept.name: Matrix Traversal Patterns

relationships.description: Connects Matrix Traversal Patterns to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Matrix traversal patterns govern how algorithms walk 2D arrays—via row-major sweeps, 4/8-directional BFS/DFS, multi-source wavefronts, spiral/diagonal scans, or 2D prefix sums—balancing asymptotic complexity with L1 cache locality.
spark.keyTakeaway: Choosing the right traversal order (row-major for cache hits, multi-source BFS for shortest grid distances, 2D prefix sums for O(1) submatrix queries) cuts latency by 10x–60x.

concept.whyItMatters: 2D grids underpin image convolutions, pathfinding, dynamic programming tables, and dense linear algebra. Even when two algorithms share `O(R · C)` time complexity, striding against memory layout (column-major in C/Java/NumPy) or running repeated single-source BFS turns a 2 ms pass into a 120 ms cache-miss bottleneck.
whenToUse: Grid shortest-path, flood-fill, and connected-component problems (4-directional or 8-directional BFS/DFS).
Multi-origin propagation (nearest exit, fire spread, distance to nearest 0) using simultaneous multi-source BFS.
Repeated rectangular region queries (`sumRegion(r1, c1, r2, c2)`) via 2D prefix sums or dense image/DP sweeps.
whenNotToUse: Ultra-sparse graphs (e.g., 10,000 nodes with 20,000 edges) where an `O(V²)` adjacency matrix wastes 99% of memory and iteration time compared to an adjacency list.
Unbounded continuous coordinate spaces where quadtrees, R-trees, or spatial hashing avoid materializing huge empty grids.
Recursive DFS on grids larger than ~10,000 cells in languages without tail-call optimization (Python/Java), where stack overflow is guaranteed.
keyPoints: Row-major traversal (`for r: for c:`) streams contiguous 64-byte cache lines with hardware prefetching, running 20x–60x faster than column-major traversal on large C/Java/NumPy arrays.
Multi-source BFS enqueues all starting cells at `dist = 0` before popping, computing shortest distances from any source in a single `O(R · C)` pass instead of `O(K · R · C)`.
0-1 BFS (using a `deque`) solves grids with `{0, 1}` edge weights in `O(R · C)` time—faster than Dijkstra's `O(R · C log(R · C))`.
Diagonal traversals exploit constant `r + c` (anti-diagonals) and `r - c` (main diagonals) invariants; spiral traversals shrink four boundary pointers (`top, bottom, left, right`).
2D Prefix Sums (`P[r+1][c+1] = grid[r][c] + P[r][c+1] + P[r+1][c] - P[r][c]`) answer any submatrix sum query in `O(1)` after `O(R · C)` preprocessing.

examples.title: Cache-Friendly Image Convolution & Transpose
examples.scenario: A Python/C++ service transposes and convolves 4096×4096 `float64` satellite tiles (128 MB each, exceeding L3 cache).
examples.outcome: Switching from naive column-major access to 32×32 cache-blocked (tiled) traversal reduced L1/L3 cache misses by 94% and cut tile processing time from 410 ms to 28 ms.

examples.title: Multi-Source BFS for Warehouse Robot Routing
examples.scenario: A 2,000×2,000 warehouse grid must compute the distance from every floor cell to the nearest of 150 charging stations.
examples.outcome: Replacing 150 separate BFS runs with a single multi-source BFS seeded with all 150 stations dropped compute time from 11.4 seconds to 78 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Iterative BFS/DFS with an explicit `deque`/`ArrayDeque` never overflows the call stack on 1000×1000 grids.
tradeOffs.con: Requires slightly more boilerplate to manage explicit state frames.

tradeOffs.pro: Mutating the grid (e.g., `grid[r][c] = -1` or bitmasking) saves `O(R · C)` auxiliary memory.
tradeOffs.con: Destroys input data for concurrent readers unless restored or bit-masked carefully.

tradeOffs.factor: 2D Prefix Sum Preprocessing vs. Direct Scan
tradeOffs.pro: Reduces each rectangular sum query from `O(R · C)` to `O(1)`.
tradeOffs.con: Static only: each cell update forces `O(R · C)` rebuild unless upgraded to a 2D Fenwick Tree (`O(log R · log C)`).

failureModes.name: Call-Stack Overflow in Recursive DFS
failureModes.description: A snake-like path on a 500×500 grid reaches recursion depth 250,000, crashing Python (`RecursionError` at 1,000) or Java (`StackOverflowError`).
failureModes.mitigation: Use an explicit iterative stack/deque for DFS or BFS on any grid larger than 32×32.

failureModes.name: Late Visited Marking (BFS Memory Explosion)
failureModes.description: Marking `visited[nr][nc] = true` when *popping* from the BFS queue instead of when *pushing* causes the same cell to be enqueued multiple times, blowing up memory exponentially.
failureModes.mitigation: Always mark cells as visited immediately before `queue.append((nr, nc))`.

failureModes.name: Column-Major Cache Thrashing
failureModes.description: Iterating `for c in cols: for r in rows:` on a 4096×4096 `int64` matrix jumps 32 KB per step, causing a cache miss on almost every read.
failureModes.mitigation: Traverse row-major (`for r: for c:`) or use cache-oblivious/tiled 32×32 blocks for transposes and DP.

failureModes.name: Boundary Off-by-One in Spiral / Diagonal Sweeps
failureModes.description: Shrinking `top/bottom/left/right` bounds without re-checking `top <= bottom && left <= right` double-visits the center row/column of odd-dimension matrices.
failureModes.mitigation: Guard the reverse bottom/left loops with explicit `if top <= bottom` and `if left <= right` checks.

commonMistakes: Mutating or checking `grid[r][c]` before validating `0 <= r < R and 0 <= c < C`.
Using `list.pop(0)` in Python for BFS (`O(N)` shift) instead of `collections.deque.popleft()` (`O(1)`).
Confusing `grid[row][col]` indexing with Cartesian `(x, y)` coordinates.
Using standard BFS on a weighted grid instead of 0-1 BFS (deque) or Dijkstra (min-heap).
Ignoring integer overflow in 2D prefix sums on large `int32` matrices (use `int64`/`long`).

sections.content:
## The idea

Matrix traversal is the art of choosing a **visitation schedule** over a 2D coordinate space `(r, c)` that matches both the algorithm's dependency order and the CPU's memory layout.

In row-major languages (C, C++, Java, Python/NumPy, Rust), element `(r, c)` sits immediately adjacent to `(r, c + 1)`. A linear row sweep loads 8 `int64` values per 64-byte cache line (~0.4 ns/element), whereas jumping down columns triggers L1/L2/L3 cache misses (~12–25 ns/element). Beyond hardware locality, specialized schedules—**multi-source BFS**, **0-1 BFS**, **diagonal (`r ± c`) sweeps**, **spiral boundary peeling**, and **2D prefix sums**—collapse multi-pass work into single `O(R · C)` passes.

## Concrete walkthrough

Walk through **Multi-Source BFS** to compute each cell's distance to the nearest gate (`0`) around walls (`-1`) in an `R × C` grid:

1. **Seed Phase**: Scan the grid once in row-major order. Push every gate `(r, c)` with `grid[r][c] == 0` into a `deque` (already marked at distance `0`).
2. **Wavefront Expansion**: Pop `(r, c)` from the front of the `deque`. For each of the 4 neighbors `(nr, nc)` via `dirs = [(0,1),(1,0),(0,-1),(-1,0)]`, verify bounds `0 <= nr < R` and `0 <= nc < C`.
3. **Mark-on-Push Invariant**: If `grid[nr][nc] == INF` (unvisited open room), immediately set `grid[nr][nc] = grid[r][c] + 1` *before* pushing `(nr, nc)` to the back of the `deque`.
4. **Termination**: Because all distance-`d` cells are processed before any distance-`d+1` cell, the first time any cell is reached is guaranteed optimal in `O(R · C)` time and `O(R · C)` worst-case queue space.

sections.content:
## Cache locality, tiling & diagonal invariants

Three structural tricks separate naive grid loops from systems-grade implementations:

- **Loop Tiling (Blocking)**: For operations that read both rows and columns (matrix transpose, Floyd-Warshall, `C = A × B`), process `B × B` sub-blocks (e.g., `B = 32` or `64` fitting inside 32 KB L1D cache) so both source and destination lines stay resident.
- **Diagonal Keys**: Cells on the same top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal share `r - c = const`; cells on the same anti-diagonal share `r + c = const`. Grouping or indexing by `r ± c` turns diagonal scans into `O(1)` bucket lookups.
- **In-Place State Encoding**: When values are bounded (e.g., `0` or `1` in Game of Life), pack `next_state` into bit 1 (`val |= next << 1`) during the pass and right-shift (`val >>= 1`) in a cleanup pass for `O(1)` extra space.

## Comparing matrix traversal patterns

| Pattern | Time Complexity | Aux Space | Ideal Use Case | Key Invariant |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Row-Major / Tiled Sweep** | `O(R · C)` | `O(1)` | Convolutions, transpose, DP tables | Sequential 64B cache-line prefetch |
| **Multi-Source BFS** | `O(R · C)` | `O(R · C)` | Unweighted shortest path to nearest target | Mark `visited` on push, not pop |
| **0-1 BFS (Deque)** | `O(R · C)` | `O(R · C)` | Grids with `{0, 1}` movement cost | Push `0`-cost to front, `1`-cost to back |
| **Iterative DFS** | `O(R · C)` | `O(R · C)` | Flood fill, island counting, cycle detection | Explicit stack avoids call-stack overflow |
| **Spiral / Boundary Peel** | `O(R · C)` | `O(1)` | Layer rotation, spiral serialization | Guard `top <= bottom` & `left <= right` |
| **2D Prefix Sum** | `O(R·C)` build, `O(1)` query | `O(R · C)` | Static rectangular sum/count queries | Inclusion-exclusion on `(r+1, c+1)` |

## Failure modes

1. **Queue Blowup from Mark-on-Pop**: In a diamond-shaped open grid, marking `visited` on pop lets each cell be pushed by up to 2–4 neighbors, causing `O(2^(R+C))` queue growth. *Mitigation*: Mark `visited` at enqueue time.
2. **Python `RecursionError` / JVM `StackOverflowError`**: Recursive DFS on a 1000×1000 grid hits depth 10^6. *Mitigation*: Always convert grid DFS to an explicit iterative stack.
3. **`O(N)` Queue Pop Overhead**: Using `ArrayList.remove(0)` or Python `list.pop(0)` degrades BFS from `O(R · C)` to `O((R · C)^2)`. *Mitigation*: Use `collections.deque` or `java.util.ArrayDeque`.
4. **Integer Overflow in 2D Prefix Sums**: Summing `int32` pixels across a 4096×4096 grid overflows signed 32-bit integers. *Mitigation*: Store prefix arrays in `int64` / `long`.

## 0-1 BFS & A* heuristics on grids

When grid edges have non-uniform costs, avoid defaulting blindly to Dijkstra:

- **0-1 BFS**: If every step costs `0` (e.g., matching arrow direction) or `1` (changing direction), push `0`-cost neighbors to the **front** of a `deque` and `1`-cost neighbors to the **back**. This preserves sorted frontier order in `O(R · C)` without a `log(R · C)` heap.
- **A* with Manhattan/Chebyshev Heuristic**: For single-source single-target routing on large open maps, adding admissible `h(r, c) = |r - tr| + |c - tc|` (4-dir) or `max(|r - tr|, |c - tc|)` (8-dir) prunes > 80% of off-target wavefront cells.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify `(r, c)` bounds (`0 <= r < R`, `0 <= c < C`) before indexing.
- [ ] Iterate row-major (`r` outer, `c` inner) or use cache-tiled blocks for large matrices.
- [ ] Use iterative `deque` / `ArrayDeque` for BFS/DFS on grids larger than 32×32.
- [ ] Mark cells visited (or update distance) **on push**, never on pop.
- [ ] Use `int64`/`long` for 2D prefix sums and test edge cases: `1×1`, `1×N`, `N×1`, and all-walls grids.

nodes.label: Shortest-Distance Grid
nodes.role: Every cell holds min hops to gate

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Matrix traversal patterns govern how algorithms walk 2D arrays—via row-major sweeps, 4/8-directional BFS/DFS, multi-source wavefronts, spiral/diagonal scans, or 2D prefix sums—balancing asymptotic complexity with L1 cache locality.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: 4-Dir Neighbor Guard applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Shortest-Distance Grid.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Shortest-Distance Grid experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use an explicit iterative stack/deque for DFS or BFS on any grid larger than 32×32.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Choosing the right traversal order (row-major for cache hits, multi-source BFS for shortest grid distances, 2D prefix sums for O(1) submatrix queries) cuts latency by 10x–60x.
Avoid trap: Mutating or checking `grid[r][c]` before validating `0 <= r < R and 0 <= c < C`.
Avoid trap: Using `list.pop(0)` in Python for BFS (`O(N)` shift) instead of `collections.deque.popleft()` (`O(1)`).
When to reach for it: Grid shortest-path, flood-fill, and connected-component problems (4-directional or 8-directional BFS/DFS).
When to reach for it: Multi-origin propagation (nearest exit, fire spread, distance to nearest 0) using simultaneous multi-source BFS.

putItTogether.title: Putting Matrix Traversal Patterns Together
putItTogether.summary: Choosing the right traversal order (row-major for cache hits, multi-source BFS for shortest grid distances, 2D prefix sums for O(1) submatrix queries) cuts latency by 10x–60x.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Matrix Traversal Patterns before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Switching from naive column-major access to 32×32 cache-blocked (tiled) traversal reduced L1/L3 cache misses by 94% and cut tile processing time from 410 ms to 28 ms.
